name: Stockholm
title: Holidays in Stockholm
intro: A city built on islands, with candlelit Christmas markets, Lucia processions and a museum about Pippi Longstocking. Here's what Stockholm is like, when to go and how long to stay.
facts_note: The EU is bringing in new entry checks, so check the rules on GOV.UK before you book.
when_to_go: Late November to Christmas brings markets and lights, with Lucia celebrations on 13 December. May to August is warm with very long days, perfect for island-hopping. January and February are cold, dark and quiet.

things.name: Gamla Stan Christmas market
things.blurb: Red huts in Stortorget, the old town's main square, sell glögg, gingerbread and smoked reindeer.

things.name: Skansen
things.blurb: An open-air museum with Nordic animals and a traditional Christmas market on Advent weekends.

things.name: Junibacken
things.blurb: A storybook museum about Astrid Lindgren's books, with a little train ride through the stories.

things.name: Vasa Museum
things.blurb: A huge 17th-century warship that sank on her first voyage and was raised almost whole.

things.name: Lucia Day
things.blurb: On 13 December, choirs in white robes with candles in their hair sing in churches and halls all over the city.

things.name: Archipelago boat trip
things.blurb: Ferries weave between thousands of islands. Best from May to September.

faqs.question: Is Stockholm good for a family holiday?
faqs.answer: Yes. It's safe and easy to get around, and the museums are among Europe's best for children.

faqs.question: When are the Christmas markets on?
faqs.answer: Gamla Stan's market usually runs from late November to 23 December. Skansen's opens on Advent weekends.

faqs.question: Is Stockholm expensive?
faqs.answer: Fairly, especially eating out. Museums like Junibacken and the Vasa are worth the money, and a travel card saves on transport.

faqs.question: How dark is it in December?
faqs.answer: It's light for only about six hours, so plan outdoor things for the middle of the day.
